flowRoot.flowPara: Application issues multiple reads (good) or writes (questionable) in parallel. OpenZGY must at least be thread safe (use locks where needed) but performance improvement is only achieved by letting I/O or compression or preferably both run in parallel.

It depends on the application whether multi threading should be done at this level (application needs code to parallelize requests) or inside OpenZGY (application needs to send large requests to get good performance). Possibly a mix of both methods may be used, but that might cause issues with number of threads. SOMEBODY FIND OUT WHAT PETREL PREFERS!

Only good for parallelizing compression, and that is easier to do at a lower level. May result in slower I/O on read if the bricks get scrambled on the file. I.e. the application needs to be very careful here. Even with that problem solved, OpenZGY will in any case need to buffer writes until it has enough for one segment. Which means that any multi-threading from application code might not have much effect

No requirements for the application. Compression and decompression is speeded up by offloading this task to a GPU. This makes the entire application dependent on libraries (nvidia, opencl, whatever) and can have a huge impact on devops unless the application already uses the GPU. Also, last time I checked the best compression algorithm that ZFP offers is not supported on GPU. So we might lose some quality

No requirements for the application. Compression and decompression is speeded up by parallelizing individual 64^3 bricks. This is fairly easy to implement. ZFP supports this internally. But testing suggests the threading overhead will be too large. And it won't play well with other ways of parallelizing compression.
Not useful because SDAPI already allows reading part of a brick in multiple threads. Having the calling layer do the parallelizing is more efficient.
SDAPI might use some GCS or Azure tricks to parallelize uploads to a single brick. That would be transparent to the caller. But, I can get similar results by writing smaller bricks..
Application needs to send large requests to get good performance. OpenZGY internally splits it into chunks and does multi-threading.

The Finalize stage (generating low resolution bricks) can be viewed as a separate application doing read/write on the ZGY file. As such it can benefit from all the "Good idea" boxes. Parallelizing at the higher level might not be useful though. It won't apply to writes (flagged as a bad idea). Also the finalize code is more efficient the more memory it is allowed to use. With memory being a finite resource this means that each thread will have less memory to work with.

Probably the best approach here is to use today's single threaded code that fills a large buffer before writing out the buffer to a single object. Except that when it is time for the actual write the code changes its mind about the segment size making it e.g.1/8th of what it used to be and then writing those 8 segments in parallel. These writer threads can be detached from the rest of the logic meaning that lod reading and computing may continue while writes are pending. Exception: If there is application does misaligned access and that triggers a read/modify/write and that requires data from a pending write then a lock will cause the main thread to wait for the pending write to complete. This is a non-typical scenario so the only issue here is that it might be difficult to test. Caveat: All of this assumes that SDAPI is thread safe on writes. TODO-High: This needs to be verified.

Another (but questionable) approach is to keep the segment size unchanged but to allow more than one open segment. This would be more flexible as the number of writer threads could vary dynamically. And a single writer thread that happens to take a very long time (e.g. due to a retry) won't end up holding up the rest. But, the read/modify/write logic and related locking might end up really complex just to get some probably small performance gain.

There are a few places in the finalize code where additional concurrency is possible. Especially where 4 brick-columns are combined into one. This would always be just 2x or 4x parallelization. And given that there will be multi threading also at the layer above, this ides might not have merit.
Weighted average is by far the most expensive algorithm, even more so than the low pass filter.
